title: Invariant: Always True
story: Your game's Health struct has two fields: current (50) and maximum (100). But a bug sets current to 150 — more than maximum! That makes no sense. You need a rule that's ALWAYS true, no matter what happens: 'current must be between 0 and maximum.' In XIOM, that's an `invariant:` — a condition checked after every single mutation to the struct, forever.
why: Invariants guarantee data integrity across ALL operations — no matter how many methods or mutations happen, the struct can never enter an invalid state.
analogy: An invariant is like a safety railing on a balcony. You can lean against it, walk near it, even bump into it — but you can't fall off, even if you try. The Health invariant (`current >= 0` AND `current <= maximum`) is the railing: you can deal damage, heal, reset — but current can NEVER go below 0 or above maximum. The railing is checked after EVERY action. No action, no matter how buggy, can push you over the edge.
try_it: Create a `Temperature` type with `celsius: Float64; invariant: celsius >= -273.15;` (absolute zero). Write `set_celsius` and `set_fahrenheit` methods that both respect the invariant. Try creating `Temperature { celsius: -500.0 }` — the invariant should trap. Write a `Speed` type with `meters_per_second: Float64; invariant: meters_per_second >= 0.0;`. Add a `brake` method that decreases speed but never below 0. What happens if your `brake` method has a bug and returns -5? The invariant catches it.
tips: Invariants are checked after construction AND after every method call — they're the ultimate safety net
Use invariants for relationships between fields: `current <= maximum`, `start <= end`
If a method can't maintain the invariant, the method must adjust its logic — the invariant is non-negotiable
common_mistakes: Writing an invariant that's too weak — `invariant: value >= -1000000;` is true but useless
Writing an invariant that conflicts with a method's normal operation — the method must always satisfy the invariant
Expecting invariants to be checked during method execution (between lines) — they're only checked at method boundaries (before/after)
